lesson.title: Why Every Indefinite Integral Needs a Plus C
lesson.summary: The constant of integration, written C, exists because the derivative of any constant is zero, which means infinitely many functions share the same derivative.
lesson.body:
Every indefinite integral you have written so far has ended with '+ C.' It is time to explain precisely why that C is not optional decoration but a mathematical necessity.

The reason traces back to one fact about derivatives: the derivative of a constant is always zero. If k is any constant number, d/dx[k] = 0, because a constant function never changes, so its rate of change is zero everywhere. This has a surprising consequence when you run differentiation in reverse. If F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x), then F(x) + k is also an antiderivative of f(x) for any constant k, because adding a constant to F does not change its derivative at all.

Let's see this directly. Take F(x) = x^2 and G(x) = x^2 + 7. Differentiate both: d/dx[x^2] = 2x, and d/dx[x^2 + 7] = 2x + 0 = 2x. Both functions have exactly the same derivative, 2x, even though F and G are different functions that never take the same value. Geometrically, the graph of G is just the graph of F shifted straight up by 7 units, and a vertical shift never changes the steepness of a curve at a given x-value, which is precisely what the derivative measures.

Because this works for any constant, not just 7, there is no single antiderivative of 2x. There is an entire vertical stack of them: x^2, x^2 + 7, x^2 - 3, x^2 + 1000, and so on, forever. The constant of integration, C, is how we represent 'any constant at all' in one symbol, so that ∫2x dx = x^2 + C captures every member of that infinite stack simultaneously. Leaving off the C is not a minor omission; it silently claims there is only one antiderivative when in fact there are infinitely many, so it changes the meaning of the answer.
